question: Does the element-mean reduction let metal-centred few-atom clouds dominate the fm_term gradient?

cohort.mode: eval() + torch.no_grad() — forward passes only, no training
cohort.determinism: The seed fixes x0 and t, but the EGNN forward is not bit-exact across runs on CUDA: two invocations at seed 1234 agreed to ~7e-8 relative on all three reductions (MEASURED). Every conclusion below is far outside that band.

reductions_over_the_same_residuals.a_note: sum_c n_c*3*mean_c / (3*sum_c n_c) — this is what F.mse_loss returns and therefore what fm_term in the trainer's _LAST_LOSS_TERMS is.
reductions_over_the_same_residuals.a_equals_note: a is the atom-count-weighted mean of per-cloud element means; trainer_F_mse_loss is the mean over batches of torch's own F.mse_loss(vel, target_dx). They differ only by batch-mean vs global-mean; the reduction is IDENTICAL (mean over N*3 elements).

floor_and_attribution.definition: per-element MSE of the trivial predictor v(x,t,z)==0, i.e. E|x1-x0|^2, on the SAME draws
floor_and_attribution.note_variance_of_target: target_dx = x1 - x0 with x0 ~ N(0, sigma^2) and sigma = 2.485, so E|target|^2/3 = sigma^2 + E|x1|^2/3 = 12.3627 MEASURED here. A perfect conditional-mean predictor cannot reach 0; it reaches E[Var(x1 - x0 | x_t, t, z)].

verdict.hypothesis: F.mse_loss averages over all elements, so a cloud with few atoms and a tight metal centre dominates the gradient while the organic ligand branch contributes almost nothing; the fix would be a per-cloud normalisation.
why_not: The reduction barely matters: (a) element-mean 9.3250 vs (b) cloud-mean 8.9480, a 4.2% gap. A per-cloud normalisation would move the objective by ~4%, not the ~10x the hypothesis needs.

The sign is wrong. Pearson(loss, n_atoms) = +0.408 — LARGER clouds have HIGHER per-element loss, so the element-mean reduction up-weights big organic complexes, not small metal centres. Pearson(loss, ligand radius of gyration) = +0.696.
Small clouds do NOT own the gradient. The 23 clouds with n_atoms <= 25 hold 6.6% of the atoms and 4.9% of the gradient under (a) — they are UNDER-represented, not dominant.
Metal atoms are almost free. 192 metal atoms (2.6% of atoms) carry 1.0% of the squared error; their per-element MSE is 3.76 vs 9.47 for the 7250 ligand atoms.
Concentration is mild and top-HEAVY, not tail-heavy: the top 10% of clouds hold 21.9% of the gradient under (a) and 16.3% under (b), against a uniform 10%.
verdict.what_the_data_shows_instead: Loss rises with molecule size because the TARGET's own scale does: Pearson(loss, zero-predictor MSE on the same cloud) = +0.685, and normalising by it collapses the size effect (Pearson(loss/zero, ligand radius) falls 0.696 -> 0.197). Pearson(loss, t) = +0.076 and eta for metal identity = 0.092, so neither the flow time nor which metal it is explains the variance. The remaining live signal is the mid-interpolant band: t in [0.4,0.6) scores 11.63 against 7.19 at t<0.2.
verdict.why_fm_term_moves_slowly: MEASURED: the model removes only 24.6% of the trivial v==0 predictor's loss (9.325 vs 12.363 per element). Most of 12.46 is the variance of the regression target itself, not a failure to fit. Both subsets are equally far from the floor: 25.4% of zero-predictor loss removed below median carbon, 24.1% at or above — no subset is being neglected.
verdict.recommended_action: DO NOT change the reduction. It is worth ~4% and no subset is starved. The measured lever is the mid-interpolant band (t in [0.4,0.8) carries 43.9% of the gradient at the highest per-element loss), so if anything moves, weight t — which is a sampling-distribution change (Karras sigma weighting), not a reduction change, and would need its own A/B.

floor_on_principle.status: REASONING, not measurement — but the zero-predictor baseline above IS measured and bounds it.
floor_on_principle.argument: target_dx = x1 - x0 with x0 ~ N(0, sigma^2 I), sigma = 2.485. Conditioned on (x_t, t, z) the target is stochastic whenever the corpus has more than one molecule consistent with that state, so the Bayes-optimal MSE is E[Var(x1 - x0 | x_t, t, z)], strictly positive. The ceiling on any fix is that quantity, and the measured v==0 baseline of 12.363 per element is an UPPER bound on it (a perfect predictor scores 0; v==0 scores the raw target second moment).
floor_on_principle.measured_anchor: E|target|^2/3 = sigma^2 + E|x1|^2/3 = 12.363 MEASURED at sigma=2.485. The model sits at 9.325, i.e. 75.4% of that upper bound. The irreducible share is unknown from this measurement alone — an oracle conditional-mean predictor would be needed to separate 'reducible' from 'conditional variance'.
floor_on_principle.citation: arXiv:2506.03719 (conditional variance at (x_t, t) is the irreducible CFM regression floor); the sigma-matched prior here follows EDM arXiv:2203.17003.
